questions.prompt: Why does ICP need a good initial guess?
options: Because SVD is numerically unstable for large rotations
The cost is non-convex: nearest-neighbour correspondences are only right when the clouds are already close, so ICP converges to the *local* minimum of whatever basin it starts in
Because the Kabsch solution is only valid for small angles
It doesn't; ICP is globally optimal with enough iterations
questions.explanation: Each iteration is optimal *given* the correspondences (Kabsch is exact for any rotation), but the correspondences come from a greedy nearest-neighbour guess. Far from the truth, most pairs are wrong and the iteration settles in a wrong basin (typically within ~20–30° / a fraction of the scene scale). Remedies: a motion prior (IMU, constant velocity, wheel odometry), global registration first (FPFH + RANSAC, TEASER++), coarse-to-fine voxel pyramids, or Go-ICP (branch & bound) when you really need global optimality.

options: Only the missing reflection check is wrong
Both: t must be `q_mean - R * p_mean`, and R may have det = -1 without the diag(1,1,det(VUᵀ)) correction
Nothing; it should be `U * V^T` though
questions.explanation: Two classic bugs. (1) With centred data the optimal translation is $t = \bar q - R\bar p$. `q̄ − p̄` is only right when R = I. (2) $VU^\top$ is the best *orthogonal* matrix, which can be a reflection (det −1) for planar or very noisy data. Fix: $R = V\,\mathrm{diag}(1,1,\det(VU^\top))\,U^\top$. With $H = \sum \tilde p\tilde q^\top$ the order is $VU^\top$. If you define $H=\sum \tilde q \tilde p^\top$ it becomes $UV^\top$, so know your convention.

questions.prompt: Point-to-plane ICP with $R\approx I+[\omega]_\times$, $t=v$, $\delta=(\omega,v)$. What is the $1\times 6$ Jacobian of $r_i = n_i\cdot(Rp_i + t - q_i)$ at $\delta = 0$?
questions.explanation: $n\cdot(\omega\times p) = \omega\cdot(p\times n)$ (scalar triple product), so $\partial r/\partial\omega = (p\times n)^\top$ and $\partial r/\partial v = n^\top$. Note the order: $n\times p$ flips the sign and is a classic bug. Then $H=\sum J^\top J$, $b=\sum J^\top r$, $\delta=-H^{-1}b$, and update $T \leftarrow \mathrm{Exp}(\delta)\,T$.

questions.prompt: A robot drives down a long featureless corridor. Your point-to-plane ICP returns a pose that drifts along the corridor axis. How do you *detect* this in the solver?
options: The smallest eigenvalue of $H = J^\top J$ is tiny relative to the largest; its eigenvector points along the corridor (translation)
questions.explanation: The walls and floor constrain only the directions their normals span; translation along the corridor changes no residual, so $H$ is (near-)singular in that direction. RMSE can be *small* because everything fits. Detect it via the eigenvalues of $H$ (or its condition number), then don't update along that eigenvector (LOAM's 'solution remapping'), fuse wheel odometry or IMU there, or flag the result as degenerate.

questions.prompt: Point-to-point vs point-to-plane vs GICP / NDT. Which statement is right?
options: Point-to-point converges fastest on structured indoor scenes
Point-to-plane lets points slide along surfaces, which removes the zig-zag of point-to-point and typically converges in far fewer iterations, but needs target normals
questions.explanation: Point-to-point penalises in-plane offsets that are just sampling differences, so it converges slowly (linearly) on planar scenes. Point-to-plane only penalises distance along the normal, so it converges in a few iterations with near-quadratic behaviour when close. GICP models both clouds as local Gaussians (plane-to-plane, needs per-point covariances). NDT matches points to per-voxel Gaussians of the target, so no explicit NN correspondences are needed.

questions.prompt: Scan-to-map odometry with a constant-velocity prior. Poses are world-from-body. Given the previous two poses $T_{k-2}, T_{k-1}$, the prediction for $T_k$ is:
questions.explanation: The last body-frame motion is $\Delta = T_{k-2}^{-1}T_{k-1}$; replay it on the right: $T_k \approx T_{k-1}\Delta$. Option A applies the motion in the world frame, which is wrong when the robot has turned. Option C isn't even in SE(3). Option D is the relative motion itself, not a pose. KISS-ICP uses exactly this prior, and it's also the basis for constant-velocity deskewing.

questions.prompt: Why do most lidar odometry systems register each scan to a **local map** rather than to the previous scan?
options: The previous scan is too dense
A local map makes ICP globally optimal
The map is denser and more complete, so correspondences are better and errors don't compound scan-to-scan; drift grows much more slowly
questions.explanation: Scan-to-scan suffers from sparse, partially overlapping lidar rings and accumulates every pairwise error. A local map (voxel hash in KISS-ICP, ikd-tree in FAST-LIO2, edge/plane maps in LOAM) aggregates many keyframes, which averages noise and gives full overlap. Keep it bounded: insert only at keyframes (distance/angle thresholds), cap points per voxel, and drop voxels beyond max range.

questions.prompt: Your ICP must run at 10 Hz on a 128-beam lidar (~250k points/scan) on one CPU core. What's the most effective first step?
options: Voxel-downsample the scan (and keep the map voxelised) so ICP works on a few thousand points, then use a KD-tree or voxel-hash NN
Increase the number of ICP iterations
questions.explanation: The cost is dominated by (#points × #iterations × NN cost). Downsampling 250k → ~5–10k points (adaptive voxel size), plus O(1)/O(log N) NN, buys 1–2 orders of magnitude. The 3×3 SVD is negligible. Then add early termination on Δpose, a good initial guess (fewer iterations) and parallel correspondence search (OpenMP/TBB).
